title: Unit 4: Cell Communication and Cell Cycle

topics.name: The cell cycle and its regulation

guide.title: Cell communication and cell cycle: review guide
guide.intro: Cells send and receive signals to coordinate their activities, keep conditions stable with feedback, and divide in a controlled cycle. This unit covers signaling pathways, feedback, the cell cycle, and what happens when its controls fail.

sections.title: Cell communication and signal transduction
body: Cells communicate by direct contact (such as gap junctions), by local signals that act on nearby cells (paracrine), and by hormones carried long distances in the blood (endocrine).

Signaling has three stages: reception (a ligand binds a specific receptor), transduction (a relay of molecules, often a phosphorylation cascade of protein kinases and second messengers such as cAMP, carries and amplifies the signal), and response (such as changing gene expression or enzyme activity). Nonpolar ligands such as steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell.
points: One signal molecule can activate many molecules downstream (amplification).
Mutations in receptors or relay proteins can block signaling or leave it stuck on.
Signals are turned off by enzymes such as phosphatases.

sections.title: Feedback
body: Negative feedback returns a variable toward a set point: high blood glucose triggers insulin release, cells take up glucose, and as glucose falls, insulin release falls. It maintains homeostasis.
Positive feedback amplifies a change and moves the system further from its starting point, usually toward an endpoint, as in contractions during childbirth (oxytocin) or fruit ripening (ethylene).
points: Most homeostatic controls are negative feedback.
Positive feedback loops end when the process is complete.
If target cells stop responding to a signal, the regulated variable stays out of range.

sections.title: The cell cycle and its regulation
body: The cell cycle has interphase (G₁ growth, S phase DNA replication, G₂ preparation) and the mitotic phase (mitosis, then cytokinesis). Mitosis makes two genetically identical nuclei. Cells that stop dividing, such as most nerve cells, leave the cycle and enter G₀.

Checkpoints (G₁, G₂, and M) check for problems such as damaged DNA. Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) drive the cell from one stage to the next. Cancer results from mutations that disrupt this control, such as in tumor-suppressor genes like p53 or in genes for growth-signal proteins.
points: DNA content doubles during S phase.
Apoptosis (programmed cell death) removes damaged cells.
Cyclin levels rise and fall through the cycle; CDK levels stay steady.

example.prompt: A cell has 20 pg of DNA in G₁. How much does it have in G₂, and how much does each daughter cell have after mitosis and cytokinesis?
example.solution: DNA is copied in S phase, so a G₂ cell has 40 pg. Mitosis splits the copies evenly, so each daughter cell has 20 pg.

misconceptions: “A hormone affects every cell it reaches.”
Only cells with the matching receptor respond.
It means the response amplifies the change.
It is copied during S phase of interphase.
“Cancer cells divide because they have extra chromosomes.”
They divide because mutations disrupt cell-cycle control.

questions.prompt: What is the first step when a cell receives a chemical signal?
choices: The cell releases the signal into the blood
A ligand binds to a specific receptor
questions.explanation: Reception, the binding of the signal molecule to its receptor, starts the pathway.
choiceExplanations: That describes sending a signal, not receiving one.
Changing transcription is a possible response at the end.
Division may be a final response, not the first step.

questions.prompt: Insulin travels through the bloodstream to cells throughout the body. What type of signaling is this?
choices: Signaling between two touching cells' surface proteins
questions.explanation: Hormones carried in the blood to distant target cells are endocrine signals.
choiceExplanations: Gap junctions connect adjacent cells directly.
Paracrine signals act only on nearby cells.
Surface-to-surface signaling requires cells to touch.

questions.prompt: Steroid hormones bind receptors inside the cell rather than on its surface. Why?
choices: They are nonpolar, so they can diffuse through the plasma membrane
They are proteins that are moved in by active transport
They are too large for surface receptors
They are made inside the target cell
questions.explanation: Steroids are lipids, so they pass through the hydrophobic interior of the membrane.
choiceExplanations: Steroids are lipids, not proteins.
Steroids are small molecules.
Steroid hormones are made in glands and travel to target cells.

questions.prompt: How can a single hormone molecule bound to one receptor change the activity of millions of molecules in a cell?
choices: The receptor binds millions of hormone molecules at once
The hormone molecule copies itself inside the cell
Each step of the signal transduction pathway activates many molecules, amplifying the signal
The hormone is split into millions of pieces
questions.explanation: Second messengers and kinase cascades multiply the signal: one activated protein activates many at the next step.
choiceExplanations: A receptor binds one ligand at a time.
Hormones don't replicate.
The hormone isn't split up to amplify the signal.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: In many signaling pathways, protein kinases pass the signal along. What do protein kinases do?
choices: Add phosphate groups to other proteins, changing their activity
questions.explanation: Phosphorylation by kinases switches relay proteins on (or off), forming a phosphorylation cascade.
choiceExplanations: Other enzymes inactivate signals.
Removing phosphates is the job of phosphatases.
DNA polymerase copies DNA.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: A mutation leaves a relay protein in a growth-signal pathway permanently active, even when no growth signal is present. What is the most likely result?
choices: The cell keeps receiving a “divide” message and may divide uncontrollably
The cell can no longer bind the growth signal
Nothing changes, because the receptor is normal
questions.explanation: Downstream of the receptor, the pathway is stuck on, so the response happens without the signal; this is one way cancers start.
choiceExplanations: The pathway is stuck on, not off.
Binding is unaffected; the problem is downstream.
A permanently active relay protein bypasses the receptor.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: A mutation changes a receptor's binding site so the ligand can no longer bind. What happens when the ligand is present?
choices: The cell responds normally through other receptors for that ligand
The cell doesn't respond, because the pathway is never started
The ligand enters the nucleus instead
questions.explanation: Without binding there is no reception, so transduction and response don't happen.
choiceExplanations: No binding means no signal.
A receptor is specific; there isn't a backup receptor for this ligand.
A ligand that needs a surface receptor can't enter the cell this way.

choices: A response that occurs only in plants
A response that moves a variable back toward its set point
A response that harms the organism
A response that amplifies a change
questions.explanation: Negative feedback counteracts a change, maintaining homeostasis.
choiceExplanations: Negative feedback occurs in all organisms.
“Negative” refers to opposing the change, not harm.
Amplifying a change is positive feedback.

questions.prompt: During childbirth, contractions trigger the release of oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions. What kind of regulation is this?
questions.explanation: The response amplifies the original change until birth ends the loop.
choiceExplanations: Negative feedback would reduce the contractions.
Competitive inhibition involves enzymes and active sites.
Homeostasis keeps variables stable; this loop drives change.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: After a meal, blood glucose rises, insulin is released, cells take up glucose, and blood glucose falls back. Then insulin release slows. Why is this negative feedback?
choices: The response increases the original stimulus
The response (lower glucose) reduces the original stimulus (high glucose)
questions.explanation: Insulin's effect opposes the rise in glucose, returning it toward the set point.
choiceExplanations: That would be positive feedback.
Hormones can take part in either kind of feedback.
Timing doesn't define the type of feedback.

questions.prompt: In type 2 diabetes, body cells respond poorly to insulin. What would you expect to happen to blood glucose and insulin levels?
choices: Glucose stays normal because the pancreas makes more glucose
Both stay high, because glucose isn't taken up and so keeps stimulating insulin release
questions.explanation: Cells don't remove glucose well, so it stays high; high glucose keeps the pancreas releasing insulin. The feedback loop can't close.
choiceExplanations: Without a cell response, glucose doesn't fall.
The pancreas releases insulin; it doesn't make glucose to fix this.
Poor uptake keeps glucose high.

questions.prompt: During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
questions.explanation: The S (synthesis) phase of interphase copies the DNA.
choiceExplanations: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
G₁ is growth before DNA replication.
During mitosis the already-copied chromosomes are separated.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: What does mitosis followed by cytokinesis produce from one diploid cell?
questions.explanation: Mitosis separates identical copies of each chromosome, so each daughter cell gets the full set.
choiceExplanations: Four haploid cells come from meiosis.
Mitosis doesn't halve the chromosome number.
Mitosis makes two cells, and they are identical.

questions.prompt: What role do cyclins play in the cell cycle?
choices: They bind and activate cyclin-dependent kinases, which push the cell into the next stage
They pull chromosomes apart during mitosis
They form the new cell membrane during cytokinesis
They copy DNA during S phase
questions.explanation: Cyclin levels rise and fall; when enough cyclin binds its CDK, the kinase phosphorylates targets that advance the cycle.
choiceExplanations: Spindle microtubules move chromosomes.
Membrane and wall materials, not cyclins, divide the cell.
DNA polymerase copies DNA.

questions.prompt: Most mature nerve cells no longer divide. Where are they in the cell cycle?
choices: G₀, a non-dividing state outside the cycle
questions.explanation: Cells that stop dividing leave the cycle at G₁ and enter G₀.
choiceExplanations: Mitosis is a short active phase, not a resting state.
S phase is DNA replication, part of preparing to divide.
G₂ cells are preparing to divide soon.

questions.prompt: The p53 protein stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged and can trigger apoptosis. What is likely if both copies of the p53 gene are mutated?
choices: Cells with damaged DNA keep dividing, raising the risk of cancer
The cell makes extra p53 protein
questions.explanation: p53 is a tumor suppressor. Without it, the checkpoint fails and mutations accumulate in dividing cells.
choiceExplanations: p53 helps trigger repair; losing it doesn't speed repair.
Losing a brake on the cycle doesn't stop division.
Mutated genes give nonworking protein, not extra working protein.

questions.prompt: A cell has 20 pg of DNA during G₁. How much DNA does it have during G₂?
questions.explanation: DNA is replicated in S phase, so G₂ cells have twice the G₁ amount.
choiceExplanations: 10 pg is the amount in a gamete after meiosis.
80 pg doubles twice.
20 pg is the amount before replication.
